extracted.intended_audience: students and philosophers studying logic, scientific method, and the theory of definition and inference
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for forming and using definitions, identifying implicit postulates, and distinguishing genuine inference (induction/ratiocination) from mere verbal or apparent inferences. Includes rules for conversion, opposition of propositions, and the proper aims of definitional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are of names only
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions properly concern the meanings of words (names) and not directly the existence or nature of things; definitions are assertions about what a word 'means' rather than about facts which can be true or false in the same way as real propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions yield propositions about meanings (verbal propositions) and therefore are not themselves susceptible to proof or disproof as factual claims. They must be treated as conventions about language rather than as premises that assert the real existence of corresponding objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates implied in definitions are the real premises of demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition appears to serve as the premise of a demonstration, the actual premise relied on is the tacit postulate that an object (or idea) conforming to that definition exists or can be constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Euclidean demonstrations do not follow from the verbal definition of a circle but from the postulate that a figure with equal radii about a centre can be described. Always identify and make explicit the postulates that underpin purportedly definitional premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat definitions as existential premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the form 'A is B' in a definition must not be confused with asserting the real existence of an object having those properties; treating a mere definition as asserting existence can produce valid syllogisms with false conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the definition 'A dragon is a serpent breathing flame' taken as an existential premise leads to the fallacy of deriving that some serpent breathes flame. To avoid this, distinguish definitional (verbal) premises from existential factual premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: When necessary, substitute 'means' for 'is' to avoid tacit existence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the tacit assumption of real existence when using definitions, rephrase definitional claims by inserting 'means' (i.e., 'Dragon means a serpent breathing flame') so that conclusions are clearly about words or ideas, not things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device clarifies whether a syllogism is about meanings, ideas, or facts; it converts misleading existential-looking premises into explicit statements about language, producing conclusions appropriate to definitions (about words or ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about whether middle terms designate names, ideas, or things
rubrics_metrics.description: In syllogistic reasoning, the middle term must be consistently understood as referring either to a thing, to a name, or to an idea; failing to keep this distinction clear confuses what sort of conclusion legitimately follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three transformations of the 'dragon' example show different legitimate conclusions depending on whether the middle term designates a name (yielding word-meaning conclusions), an idea (yielding propositions about ideas), or things (requiring existential postulates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow only the degree of idealization required by the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates in demonstrative sciences may assert idealized properties (e.g., a circle with exactly equal radii) which are not literally realizable, but this is acceptable provided only as much of the postulate is taken as is necessary to support the portion of the conclusion that is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that mathematical definitions often idealize physical reality; the proper test is whether the factual instances or weaker postulates suffice to secure the demonstrable consequences actually claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are not arbitrary; choose connotative attributes with care
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving a distinct connotation to a general name, select attributes that are common to the important or majority of things denoted and that lead to the most interesting and useful consequences (differentiæ that yield many propriae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosopher should prefer attributes which are both widely present among the things named and of greatest explanatory or practical importance. Definitions may require deep inquiry into the nature of the things named rather than mere conventional labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for defining abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into the definition of an abstract name should (1) examine usage to see whether people agree sufficiently about what they call by the name, (2) determine whether the objects form a class at all, (3) identify common attributes running through the class, and (4) if no natural class exists, consider how best to form an artificial class the name may denote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps separate conventional/usage questions from empirical (matter-of-fact) ones and from classificatory decisions. The goal is to preserve meaningful denotation while achieving useful conceptual distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy vague or overextended names by restricting connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a name has by successive extension come to denote a confused huddle of objects and connotes nothing definite, it is unfit for thought and must be corrected by stripping away multifarious denotation and confining it to objects possessing some common attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because language 'grows' rather than being made, philosophical intervention often involves refining popular groupings rather than inventing wholly new terms; use historical/usage evidence as resources in remodelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent (verbal) inference from real inference
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparent inference is one in which the purported conclusion is merely a repetition, rephrasing, or part of what was already contained in the premise(s) (equipollency, simple conversion, deriving a particular from a universal by undeclared part-taking), and therefore affords no new proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include equating 'No man is incapable of reason' with 'Every man is rational', inferring a particular from a universal (All A is B -> Some A is B) as mere repetition, and predicate inclusion cases (Socrates is a man -> Socrates is a living creature). Such 'inferences' should not be treated as real proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversion rules correctly and understand their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain logical forms admit conversion (subject and predicate exchanged) only in specified ways: Some A is B -> Some B is A; No A is B -> No B is A; All A is B -> Some B is A (conversion per accidens). Not every form can be fully inverted (All A is B does not imply All B is A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conversion can change universality to particularity (per accidens) and that such converted propositions often assert less than the original. Misuse of conversion can create the illusion of inference where none exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular negative propositions convert by contraposition only in a modified form
rubrics_metrics.description: From Some A is not B we cannot infer directly Some B is not A; the valid conversion is to infer that something which is not B is A (i.e., convert to 'Some A is a thing which is not B' and then convert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conversion involves changing one term (to 'a thing which is not B'), so the terms of the new proposition are not simply the original predicate and subject reversed. Be cautious when handling particular negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn opposition of propositions as interpretive, not always inferential, tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical distinctions among contraries, subcontraries, contradictories, and subalterns are valuable chiefly for discerning identity of assertion under varied language and for understanding implication relations (e.g., universal truth implies particular truth), but they are not in themselves substitutes for demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms of logic help cultivate precise interpretation and the habit of measuring the scope of assertions, and thus are important preliminaries to reasoning even if they may seem deceptively obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify the real import of propositions by what they assert
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond verbal assertions about meanings, real propositions (about things) ultimately assert one or more of: Existence, Order in Place, Order in Time, Causation, or Resemblance; alternatively expressed as Subject–Attribute claims where a subject is asserted to possess or lack an attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy of what propositions assert is the foundation for understanding what sorts of proof are appropriate (e.g., proofs of existence vs. proofs of causal relations) and for analyzing whether a proposed inference can legitimately supply the asserted kind of claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define proof/inference as belief grounded on antecedent propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact or statement is said to be proved when we believe its truth by reason of some other fact or statement from which it is said to follow; to infer is to give credence to a proposition as a conclusion from previously assented premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition to check whether a purported proof indeed shows that the conclusion follows from antecedents and to distinguish genuine inferential support from mere verbal equivalence or reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate Induction and Ratiocination (syllogism) by generality of conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the process of inferring a proposition more general than the largest of the premises (ascending from particulars to generals); Ratiocination or Syllogism infers propositions equally or less general than the premises (from generals to particulars or from generals to other generals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction collects a law or principle from many instances and thus adds new content beyond the premises; ratiocination combines general propositions to derive consequences already contained in their terms. Correctly classifying the kind of inference is essential to assessing its validity and epistemic weight.
